readings.c1s2:
¶
'''well-boring''' (wel′bōr″ing), ''n.'' A method of sinking wells by drilling or boring through rock, these wells often extending to a great depth. Percussion drilling is most used for this purpose. Compare ''oil-well'', ''oil-derrick'', etc.

'''well-born''' (wel′bôrn), ''a.'' [= G. ''wohlgeboren''; as ''well''<sup>2</sup> + ''born''<sup>1</sup>.] Of high or respectable birth; not of low origin.
{{smaller block|The term ''well-born'' was a contemptuous nickname given to the Federalists.
{{right|''McMaster'', People of United States, I. 469.}}}}

'''well-breathed''' (wel′bretht), ''a.'' Long-breathed; having good wind; strong of lung.
{{smaller block|On thy ''well-breath’d'' horse keep with thy hounds.
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 678.}}}}

'''well-bred''' (wel′bred), ''a.'' '''1.''' Of good breeding; polite; cultivated; refined.
{{smaller block|<poem>For better luve I that bonnie boy
Than a’ your ''weel-bred'' men.</poem>
{{right|''Ladye Diamond'' (Child’s Ballads, II. 383).}}
<poem>A moral, sensible, and ''well-bred'' man
Will not affront me, and no other can.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Conversation, l. 193.}}}}
'''2.''' Of good breed, stock, or race, as a domestic animal. Compare ''half-bred'', ''thoroughbred''.

'''well-bucket''' (wel′buk″et), ''n.'' A vessel for drawing up water from a well: often used in pairs, one ascending while the other descends. It is usually of wood, and barrel-shaped; in some parts of Europe copper vessels are used.
{{smaller block|The muscles are so many ''well-buckets''; when one of them acts and draws, ’tis necessary that the other must obey.
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}

'''well-carriaged''' (wel′kar′ājd), ''a.'' Of good car-
readings.c1s3:
riage or deportment; well-mannered. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The mistress of the house, a pretty ''well-carriaged'' woman.
{{right|''Pepys'', Diary, I. 317.}}}}

'''well-carse†''', ''n.'' [Also Sc. ''well-kerse''; ME. ''welle carse'', < AS. ''wylle-cærse'', water-cress, < ''wylle'', well, spring, + ''cærse'', cress: see ''well''<sup>1</sup> and ''cress''.] Water-cress.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ich rede no faithful frere at thy feste sytte;
ȝut were me leuere, by oure lord, lyue by ''welle-carses''
Than haue my fode and my fyndynge of false menne wyn-
nynges.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), vii. 292.}}}}

'''well-chain''' (wel′chān), ''n.'' A chain attached to a bucket or a pair of buckets, and used with a windlass, for drawing water from a well.

'''well-conditioned''' (wel′kon-dish′ond), ''a.'' [< ME. ''well condiciond''; < ''well''<sup>2</sup> + ''conditioned''.] In good or favorable condition; in a desirable state of being: as, a ''well-conditioned'' mind. ''Prompt. Parv.'', p. 521.

'''well-conducted''' (wel′kọn-duk′ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Properly led; under good conduct: as, a ''well-conducted'' expedition.—'''2.''' Characterized by good conduct; acting well or properly; well-behaved: as, a ''well-conducted'' person or community.

'''well-curb''' (wel′kėrb), ''n.'' A curb or inclosure around and above the top of a well. See cut under ''pozzo''.
{{smaller block|Losson . . . sat on the ''well-curb'', shouting bad language down to the parrot.
{{right|''R. Kipling'', In the Matter of a Private.}}}}
readings.c2s1:
¶
'''well-deck''' (wel′dek), ''n.'' An open space on the main deck of a ship, inclosed like a well by the bulwarks and partial higher decks forward and aft.
{{smaller block|The question of the freeboard of steamers of the ''well-deck'' type is again being brought before the notice of Lloyd’s by the shipowners of the northeast coast.
{{right|''The Engineer'', LXV. 468.}}}}

'''well-decker''' (wel′dek″ėr), ''n.'' A ship having a well-deck.
{{smaller block|A large proportion of the steamers built and owned at West Hartlepool are ''well-deckers''.
{{right|''The Engineer'', LXVII. 192.}}}}

'''well-deed†''', ''n.'' [< ME. ''weldede, weldæd'', < AS. ''weldǣd'' (= OHG. ''wolatāt'' = Goth. ''wailadēds''); as ''well''<sup>2</sup> + ''deed''.] Benefit.

'''well-disposed''' (wel′dis-pōzd′), ''a.'' Of a good or favorable disposition; in a kindly or friendly state of feeling; well-willed.
{{smaller block|You lose a thousand ''well-disposed'' hearts.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., ii. 1. 206.}}
Some ''well-disposed'' persons have taken offence at my using the word Free-thinker as a term of reproach.
{{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 135.}}}}

'''well-doer''' (wel′dö′ėr), ''n.'' One who does well; a performer of good deeds or actions: opposed to ''evil-doer''.

'''well-doing''' (wel′dö′ing), ''n.'' [< ME. ''well-doing''; < ''well''<sup>2</sup> + ''doing''.] Good conduct or action.
{{smaller block|The cristin ne myght bet litill space endure, ne hadde be the ''well doinge'' of the v knyghtes.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 550.}}}}
readings.c3s1:
¶
'''well-found''' (wel′found), ''a.'' Found to be well or good; approved; commendable.
{{smaller block|<poem>Gerard de Narbon was my father;
In what he did profess ''well found.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', All’s Well, ii. 1. 105.}}
Many live comparatively ''well-found'' lives.
{{right|''Fortnightly Rev.'', N. S., XLI. 728.}}}}

'''well-founded''' (wel′foun′ded), ''a.'' Founded on good reasons; having strong probability; not baseless: as, ''well-founded'' suspicions.

'''well-given†''' (wel′giv′n), ''a.'' Given to what is well or good; well-meaning; well-intentioned.
{{smaller block|Why are you a burthen to the world’s conscience, and an eye-sore to ''well-given'' men?
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Westward Ho, ii. 2.}}}}

'''well-governor†''', ''n.'' [ME. ''wel-gouvernour'' (tr. L. ''qui bene præest'').] One who governs well.
{{smaller block|The prestis that ben ''wel gouernouris.''
{{right|''Wyclif'', 1 Tim. v. 17.}}}}

'''well-graced''' (wel′grāst), ''a.'' Held in good grace or esteem; viewed with favor; popular.
{{smaller block|<poem>The eyes of men,
After a ''well-graced'' actor leaves the stage,
Are idly bent on him that enters next.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., v. 2. 24.}}}}

'''well-grass''' (wel′grȧs), ''n.'' The water-cress, ''Nasturtium officinale.'' Also ''well-girse.'' Compare ''well-carse.'' [Scotch.]

'''well-grounded''' (wel′groun′ded), ''a.'' Having good grounds or reasons; well-based; well-founded.

'''well-head''' (wel′hed), ''n.'' The source of a natural well or spring.

[Rare.] {{smaller block|He that hath any ''well-faced'' phancy in his Crowne, and doth not vent it now, fears the pride of his owne heart will dub him dunce for ever. {{right|''N. ''Agam.'' An obsolete spelling of ''welfare.'' '''well-faring†''' (wel′fãr′ing), ''a.''   [Cf. A deep, narrow, perpendicular cavity, as the space from top to bottom of a house round which stairs turn; also, an inclosure in which a balancing-weight rises and falls, etc.—'''2.''' The well-room of a boat. '''well-house''' (wel′hous), ''n.'' A room or small house built round a well, for dairy and other domestic uses. {{smaller block|I lately had standing in my ''well-house'' . . . a great cauldron of copper. {{right|''Harman'', Caveat for Cursetors, p. 25.}}}} '''well-informed''' (wel′in-fôrmd′), ''a.'' Possessed of full information on a wide variety of subjects. '''welling''' (wel′ing), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''well''1, ''v.'']   An outpouring, as of liquid or gas. '''Wellington boot.''' '''1.''' A riding-boot with leg extending upward at the rear to the angle of the knee, and high enough in front to cover the knee. {{smaller|So called because the pattern is supposed to have been introduced by the Duke of Wellington, who wore such boots in his campaigns.}} '''2.''' A similar boot, somewhat shorter, worn under the trousers, and fitting the leg closely. {{smaller block|No gentleman could wear anything in the daytime but ''Wellington boots'', high up the leg, over which the trousers fitted tightly, covering most of the foot, and secured underneath by a broad strap. {{right|''E. Yates'', Fifty Years of London Life, I. ii.}}}} '''Wellingtonia''' (wel-ing-tō′ni-ä), ''n.''   [NL. (Lindley, 1853), named after the Duke of ''Wellington'': see ''Wellingtonian.'']   A name much used in England for the big trees of California, which has given way to the earlier name ''Sequoia'' under the rule of priority. See ''Sequoia'' (with cut). '''Wellingtonian''' (wel-ing-tō′ni-an), ''a.''   [< ''Wellington'' (see def.) + ''-ian.'']   Of or pertaining to the first Duke of Wellington (Arthur Wellesley, 1769–1852), a British general and statesman. {{smaller block|The ''Wellingtonian'' legend was once as strong in England as the Napoleonic in France. {{right|''The Academy'', No. 906, p. 159.}}}} '''well-intentioned''' (wel′in-ten′shond), ''a.'' L. L., i. 2. 77.}}}} {{smaller block|His soul ''well-knit'', and all his battles won, Mounts, and that hardly, to eternal life. {{right|''M. Arnold'', Immortality.}}}}
